The letter from the registry office
April 2036. Lena and Andrei have received a letter from the Standesamt Pankow (registry office) about registering their marriage. Ludwig reads it aloud. Andrei doesn't understand a thing.
“For the purpose of registration of the marriage, submission of the following documents is required.”
I've been speaking German for six years. I did a master's degree in German. And I don't understand a single word.
That's not German, that's officialese. Grandpa, translate, please.
It means: if you want to get married, you have to bring these papers.
Why don't they write it like that?
Because they're civil servants. Next: “In the case of foreign certificates, certification as well as translation by a sworn translator are required.”
So: Andrei's Romanian birth certificate has to be certified and translated. By someone who is authorised to do it.
“Following receipt of all documents, verification by the registry office takes place. The processing time is as a rule four weeks.”
That I understand: when they have everything, they check it, and that takes four weeks. We've still got seven weeks until the seventh of June.
And the last sentence: “If the documents are not submitted by the fifteenth of May, the desired date cannot be guaranteed.”
That means: if we don't bring the papers by the fifteenth of May, there's no wedding on the seventh of June.
I'll ring Dad right away. He has to find the birth certificate. It's somewhere among the bees.

In the nominal style, actions are expressed by nouns (die Prüfung, der Eingang, die Vorlage), not by verbs (prüfen, eingehen, vorlegen). It's typical of authorities, contracts and academic texts. It's precise and short, but hard to read.

Step 1: find the action noun (Eingang). Step 2: turn it into a verb (eingehen). Step 3: choose the right conjunction for the preposition (nach → nachdem, bei → wenn, zwecks → um … zu, trotz → obwohl, wegen → weil). Step 4: the genitive becomes the subject (der Unterlagen → die Unterlagen).
After receipt of the documents, verification takes place.
→ After the documents have arrived, they are checked.
The “empty” verbs of the nominal style (erfolgen, stattfinden, durchführen, vornehmen) often disappear in the verbal style: “Die Prüfung erfolgt” → “Sie wird geprüft”.
Because it was raining hard, the concert was cancelled.
→ Owing to the heavy rain, the concert was cancelled.
Before you leave, please hand in the key.
→ Before departure, please hand in the key.
Don't overdo the nominal style in personal letters or essays: it becomes heavy and cold. Use it when the text has to be official and short.

The letter from the Pankow registry office came on a Tuesday in mid-April, in a grey window envelope, like all the letters in Germany that make you a little bit afraid. It was two pages long, and on those two pages there were, as Elif counted later, a hundred and fourteen nouns and only nineteen verbs, eleven of which were “erfolgen”, “ist” or “wird”. Andrei read it three times. The first time he understood nothing, the second time he understood it was about the wedding, and the third time he understood there was a problem, but not which one. Then he gave the letter to Ludwig, who had worked for forty years at a state transport company and who, as he liked to say, spoke “officialese fluently, but with an accent”.

Ludwig put on his glasses and read aloud, slowly, in the solemn voice with which he used to announce the stops. After each sentence he paused and translated it into what he called “people language”. “For the purpose of registration of the marriage, submission of the following documents is required” became “Bring these papers.” “In the case of foreign certificates, certification as well as translation by a sworn translator are required” became “Andrei's papers from Romania need a stamp and have to be translated by someone who has sworn not to lie.” And “In the event of non-submission of the documents by 15 May, the desired date cannot be guaranteed” became a sentence after which the kitchen went very quiet: “If you haven't got everything by the fifteenth of May, there's no wedding on the seventh of June.”

Hotte, who of course just happened to be sitting in the kitchen, because it was Thursday, nodded wisely. “Officialese,” he said, “is a language they invented so nobody notices the official doesn't know what he wants either.” He told them about the forms he'd had to fill in in the GDR for his first Trabant, twelve pages, and how after eleven years of waiting he'd got a letter that said: “Following completion of the review of your application for the allocation of a passenger car, you are hereby informed that delivery will take place within the framework of available quotas.” Hotte paused. “Know what that meant?” he asked. “It meant: maybe. Eleven years of waitin' for a maybe.” Everyone laughed, but Andrei didn't laugh quite as loudly as the others. He was thinking about the fifteenth of May.

The problem was the birth certificate. Andrei had a copy that he had used to register in Berlin six years before, but a copy wasn't enough. The registry office wanted an original or a new, international extract from the Romanian register of births, with an apostille, a special stamp that confirms a document is genuine. The original was in Sibiu. Somewhere. Andrei rang his father that same evening and explained the problem in Romanian. Dan listened, said “Mhm” and “Da” and “Sigur”, and then said something that made Andrei go pale: “The certificate is in the box with the important papers. And the box is in the bee house.”

The bee house was a small wooden shed at the end of Dan's garden, next to the workshop where Andrei's grandfather had carved the birds. Inside there were twelve hives, and it was mid-April, the time when the bees wake up after the winter and are, as Dan said, “as bad-tempered as a civil servant on a Monday morning”. The box with the important papers stood right at the back, on a shelf, behind the third hive, because Dan was of the opinion that no thief in the world would dare to steal something by walking past twelve bee colonies. That was probably true. But it also meant that Dan himself wouldn't dare either, at least not in April, not without a protective suit, and his protective suit had had a big hole in the sleeve since last summer.

There followed two weeks that Lena later called “Operation Apostille”. Dan bought a new protective suit, which the shop in Sibiu assured him was “bee-proof according to the European standard”, and got the box out of the bee house one cool morning while the bees were still sleepy. He was stung only twice, once on the neck and once, in a way he didn't want to explain in more detail, through the supposedly bee-proof suit. In the box was the birth certificate, between Elena's school-leaving certificate, Dan's driving licence from nineteen ninety and a love letter Dan had written to Elena thirty-five years before, which Elena, when she found it, immediately confiscated. The certificate was yellowed and folded, and in one corner something was stuck that looked suspiciously like honey.

Then the bureaucracy began on the Romanian side. For the apostille, Dan had to take the original to the prefecture in Sibiu, where it was explained to him that for the apostille you first needed a new, multilingual extract from the register of births, which you get from the registry office, not from the prefecture, and that the registry office was open only on Tuesdays and Thursdays from nine to twelve. Dan arrived on Thursday at five to twelve. He got the extract the following Tuesday. With the extract he went to the prefecture, where the stamp was issued after three days. Elena said to Lena on the phone, in German, very seriously: “I thought German offices were complicated. But the Romanian offices invented the German ones.”

In Berlin, too, not everything was simple. Lena needed an extended certificate of residence from the Bürgeramt (citizens' office), and the next free appointment in the online system was, as she discovered in horror, on the twenty-third of June, two weeks after the wedding. She tried every morning at seven, when new appointments were released, with her laptop on the bakery counter, between the first rolls and the first coffee. On the sixth morning she gave up and told Dr Vogt, who was just coming off his night shift. Dr Vogt listened, drank his mint tea and said: “Bürgeramt Lichtenberg. At six fifty-three the cancelled appointments are released there. I know because at night I've got nothing else to do when there's no operation.” The next morning at six fifty-three Lena had an appointment for the following Monday. She gave Dr Vogt a whole cheesecake. He ate it, as Hotte found out later, over three nights.

On the first of May a parcel arrived on Kastanienallee from Sibiu. Inside, in a plastic sleeve, were the multilingual birth certificate with the apostille, the original, so Andrei could keep it as a memento, a jar of acacia honey and a note in Dan's large, clumsy handwriting, in German, with three mistakes that nobody corrected: “For the registry office. I was stung twice for this paper. Please marry well.” Andrei read the note and had to sit down. Then he took everything to a sworn translator in Prenzlauer Berg, a Dr Popescu, who was from Cluj, had lived in Berlin for thirty years and who, when she saw the honey stain on the original, first frowned and then smiled: “Honey. That's a first for me.”

Dr Popescu translated the certificate in one afternoon, at her old desk with a view of the Mauerpark, and while she worked she told Andrei that in thirty years she had translated more than four thousand birth certificates, Romanian, Moldovan, Hungarian. “Each one is a little story,” she said. “Name, place, date, the parents' names. That's all it says. But if you look closely, you see the midwife's hand, the village clerk's handwriting, sometimes a coffee stain. And once, in nineteen ninety-three, a certificate from Maramureș with a fingerprint in soot, because the village had no electricity.” She stamped the translation with her round seal and signed it. “Yours is the first one with honey,” she said. “I won't forget it. Good luck, Mr Ionescu. And say hello to the bees.”

On the eighth of May, a week before the deadline, Lena and Andrei stood at the Pankow registry office, in front of Mrs Kranz's office, with a folder in which every document was in a separate plastic sleeve, labelled in Elif's neat handwriting. Mrs Kranz, who was due to retire in two years and remembered Lena because she had been a witness at Mara's wedding, checked every sheet, slowly, with a pencil in her hand. She checked the birth certificates, the certificates of residence, the identity cards, the translation with Dr Popescu's round stamp. Then she picked up the original from Sibiu, the yellowed, folded one, and looked at the corner with the honey stain. “What's this?” she asked. “Honey,” said Andrei. “From my father's bees. They guarded the certificate.”

Mrs Kranz looked at him over the rim of her glasses, for a long time, with the look of an official who in thirty-two years had seen everything, forged documents, forgotten documents, documents eaten by the dog. Then she did something that, as Lena said later, wasn't in the service regulations. She took a yellow sticky note, wrote something on it and stuck it in the folder, next to the original. Then she stamped the form, signed it and pushed it across the desk. “Following verification of the documents submitted,” she said in her very best officialese, “there are no objections to the intended marriage.” And then, in people language, more quietly: “You can get married. On the seventh of June. At eleven. I'm glad.”

Lena wanted to say something and couldn't. Andrei said “Danke” in German and then once more in Romanian, “mulțumesc”, and Mrs Kranz replied, to the surprise of both of them, “cu plăcere” (you're welcome), with a slight Saxon accent. She explained that in thirty years she had married so many Romanian couples that by now she knew the most important words: “da” (yes), “mulțumesc” (thank you), “cu plăcere” (you're welcome) and “noroc” (cheers). The last one, she said, she usually heard after the ceremony, from the corridor, together with the clinking of glasses.

Outside, on the steps of the registry office, Andrei rang his father straight away. Dan was in the garden, with the bees, and Andrei could hear the buzzing in the background. He just said: “Gata, tată. Am trecut.” (Done, Dad. We're through.) We did it. At the other end there was silence for a while. Then Dan said something in Romanian that Andrei didn't translate, not even for Lena, and that, as he admitted later, he would never forget for the rest of his life. Lena didn't ask. She only asked what Mrs Kranz had written on the yellow note. Andrei didn't know. But Elif, who the next day collected the copy of the folder to bring back the plastic sleeves, saw the note and copied it, word for word, for the minutes. It said, in pencil: “Trace of honey on original. Authenticity confirmed by bees. No objections. K.”
